newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lamfalussy urges limited deviation from Maastricht.
newsitem.headline: Lamfalussy urges limited deviation from Maastricht.

text.p: European Monetary Institute president Alexandre Lamfalussy said on Tuesday any deviation from reference values stated in the Maastricht Treaty for joining European monetary union should be granted sparingly.
In a speech in Lisbon at the anniversary of the Banco de Portugal, Lamfalussy added that nations' compliance with reference values regarding debt and deficit ratios for 1997 must be sustainable.
"Deviation from the reference values should be granted sparingly by interpreting the words of the treaty in a carefully restrictive way," Lamfalussy said.
The EMI made a copy of the speech available in Frankfurt.
"Secondly, the compliance with reference values should be regarded as sufficient for eligibility only if the deficit and debt ratios observed for 1997 are genuinely sustainable," he said.

According to the Maastricht Treaty, nations wishing to join European monetary union should have a deficit level no higher than three percent of gross domestic product and a debt ceiling of 60 percent.
But, in a controversial decision, the pact also left room for deviation from those reference values under certain conditions.
The EMI president warned that since proposed European monetary union had no historic precedent, there was a risk of "things going wrong here and there."
Lamfalussy said monetary union needed to start in as strong a position as possible to help it overcome such potential difficulties.
"We should stick to both the spirit and the letter of Treaty," he said.
The EMI president said he saw some hope in the ability of nations to reduce deficit levels, and he repeated his belief that monetary union is likely to happen on schedule.
"It is fair to say that it may now be possible to detect a fiscal turnaround in most member states," he said but acknowledged more adjustment was needed.

He said that in the EU, the government debt ratio will reach an anticipated 73.5 percent in 1996, up from 56.1 percent in 1991. "It as yet shows little sign of levelling off, let alone a reversal," he said.
Lamfalussy said there were early indications that current exchange rate levels among European Union countries are sustainable.
"There are also tentative indications that current exchange rate levels are sustainable," he said.
"Evidence regarding current real exchange rates does not suggest misalignments in the ERM which could by themselves trigger major corrective forces."
But he added that caution was warranted regarding exchange rate predictions because of possible external turbulence such as swings in the U.S. dollar.
Lamfalussy said a majority within the EMI council believe a currency should belong to the Exchange Rate Mechanism before joining monetary union.
Inflationary pressures among EU countries are under control and are likely to remain tame, he said.
"In my view, there are no strong reasons for believing that current price performance is unsustainable," he said.
The EMI president said that in many EU countries, virtual price stability, or inflation of two percent or less, has been established.
He said low inflation is due to cyclical factors and the determination of EU countries to keep prices stable.

"Concerning price stability, the picture is generally favourable," he said. "On balance, one may conclude that 'home-made' inflationary processes have in many EU countries been brought largely under control."
